messages.subject: new density notation
parts:
I want to run this by everyone on stan-dev before
creating the issue and starting to work on it.

1. New density expression with normalization and vertical bar:

cauchy<norm=true>(y | mu, sigma)

defaults to norm=false:

cauchy(y | mu, sigma)


2. New increment log density statement:

ld << cauchy(tau | 0, 2.5),
normal(beta | 0, 2),
bernoulli_logit(y | x * (tau * beta));


comma-separated values all added to log density accumulator.


3.a. Deprecate the use of any function ending in "_log" and
go with the above form.

b. Maintain support for user-defined functions ending in "_log"
to be used this way and keep our density library in C++ ending in "_log".

c. Make a local variable available to functions such as norm__
with the value of the <norm=...> specification (0 or 1 as int).


4. Deprecate use of the sampling statement:

y ~ foo(theta);


5. Rewrite all the examples in the manual!


NOTE ON BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY: The proposal is to maintain backward
compatibility but raise deprecation warnings. Alternatively, we could
just capture old syntax and print specialized update warnings.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new density notation
parts:
I was thinking about just that.

* introduce "=" as a synonym for "<-" in assignment statements
and deprecate "<-"

* use "+=" for increment statements

* introduce operators "++" and "--" for expressions
- definitely prefix
- optionally postfix

Stan already includes a deprecated variable "lp__" which holds
the log density accumulator. We don't want people to assign
to that variable --- too easy to lose terms, including the Jacobian.
So we just want an increment. And we want to access its value,
and I thought we'd added a function, but I don't see it; so we need

* function log_density() that returns current value of accumulator

And then we can get rid of lp__ altogether in Stan 3.

There's the remaining question of whether we

* reserve ld as a variable or function name

It won't conflict in the streaming increment notation.
The "<<" is C++ streaming notation and we're thinking of it as streaming
additive terms to the log density accumulator.

- Bob

We'll be using it the conventional way to separate the variate/outcome
(left of bar) from parameters (right of bar). So you'd only get
normal(y | mu, sigma), not any other bar placement. And in fact
for all of our current densities, there's only argument to the left. If
we had a bivariate distribtuion that we wrote p(x, y | theta), then we'd
have a case for putting two things on the left.

It's just the way (Bayesian) statisticians write these functions. And don't
worry, Andrew, we're not going to write normal(y; mu, sigma) as an alternative
for models intended for max likelihood estimation.

> On Dec 31, 2015, at 11:20 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob!
>
> This sounds like a huge thing - is it worth investing this effort?

The biggest effort's going to be in rewriting all the doc. And
the models, but we already want to do both of those things anyway,
so now's the time to change the language. We've been discussing this
for a while and we've been holding off on updating models for this
reason. It's terrible to be frozen waiting for a big change.
> Also, the deprecation period is hopefully very long,

The deprecation may be short --- as in introducing it in 2.10 and then dropping
it some time next year when we bring out Stan 3. But so far, we don't know.
My worry is that people will keep using the old notation.

The bigger worry is that any book, etc., with a Stan model will be
out of date as soon as we do this. My impression is that I'm the one
most concerned with breaking backward compatibility, but I may be wrong.

Stan 3's the time to change things if at all (though it doesn't necessarily
mean we have to break backward compatibility).
> i.e. Stan programs will look very different wrt to BUGS programs with this.
That's a feature, not a bug (see below).

> My comments:
>
> 1. Why introduce another logic with "<norm=true/false>"? Do you plan to introduce further options here, then it makes sense. If only for discriminating between normed/unnormed I would prefer a _norm naming convention thing.

Right now,

y ~ foo(theta);

drops normalizing constants but

increment_log_prob(foo_log(y, theta));

keeps them. We'd like to be able to control the behavior on
a case-by-case behavior.

The confusing bit's still going to be that our densities are
on the unconstrained scale with Jacobians, even if they get
the normalizing constants.
> 2. What is the rationale to introduce two new operators "<<" and ","?

The rationale was to make it clearer that everything in
Stan is just incrementing a log density. So instead of having
both sampling statements and increment_log_prob statements, we
just have the log density accumulator.

The problem we have now is that people interpret the "~" as random
number generation or as graphical model building and sometimes just
copying BUGS and hoping things will work. Instead, we want to emphasize
that a Stan program is just a regular imperative program defining
a log density.

- Bob

> Maybe I haven´t understood fully, but writing
>
> lp << density1 << density2;
>
> makes more sense to me.

The notation

lp << a, b, c, d;

is from Eigen. C++ output streams would be

lp << a << b << c;

which I don't think anyone's going to like.
> In any case, I suggest to try out this new scheme on people who are more statisticians than programmers,
Andrew's the one who's been lobbying most strongly for it!
> i.e. I think someone having a programming background will absorb this easily, but I am not so sure about those people without a programming background.

Stan's a programming language, so I'm not so worried about people
who don't think they're doing programming or haven't done it before.

- Bob

When discussing the new notation, please, include examples how it will affect
functions such as
normal_cdf

normal_pdf (or normal_d?)

normal_lccdf?

>

> > 1. Why introduce another logic with "<norm=true/false>"? Do you plan to introduce further options here, then it makes sense. If only for discriminating between normed/unnormed I would prefer a _norm naming convention thing.

>
> y ~ foo(theta);
>
> drops normalizing constants but

> the normalizing constants.

> copying BUGS and hoping things will work. Instead, we want to emphasize
> that a Stan program is just a regular imperative program defining
> a log density.
>
> - Bob

> >
> > lp << density1 << density2;
> >
> > makes more sense to me.
>
> The notation
>
> lp << a, b, c, d;
>
> is from Eigen. C++ output streams would be
>
> lp << a << b << c;
>
> which I don't think anyone's going to like.
>
> > In any case, I suggest to try out this new scheme on people who are more statisticians than programmers,
>
> Andrew's the one who's been lobbying most strongly for it!
>
> > i.e. I think someone having a programming background will absorb this easily, but I am not so sure about those people without a programming background.
>
> Stan's a programming language, so I'm not so worried about people
> who don't think they're doing programming or haven't done it before.
>
> - Bob

R uses %*% for matrix multiplication, and you certainly need

C/C++/Java use | vs. || and & vs. && to differentiate bitwise

Aaaaaaah. Do we need official minutes? Almost all of these
issues were introduced in the last discussion of the proposed

> I don't think there's a consensus on what the suffixes should

> common usage.
>
> Is everyone OK with that? And with using "pdf" for both density
> and mass functions? (Yes, they're all densities with the right
> math, however the textbooks say "pmf”).

The problem with differentiating between pdfs and pmfs is that
people will get confused about whether the posterior is a pdf or
a pmf. It’s always a pdf for the models you can build in Stan,
but it’s not trivial to grok what goes where (pdfs over parameters,
hence prior or posterior, pdfs over data, pmfs over data). Then
again, being more explicit may provide an opportunity for more
clear error messages, such as when a user tries to use a pmf
over parameters.

Things become even more complicated when we use CDFs,
because they are fundamentally different from densities.

If we want to be more explicit and we don’t mind the extra typing
then I’d say go with

pdf / cdf / ccdf / dcdf
lpdf / lcdf / lccdf / ldcdf

with the understanding that not all may be implemented.

The f is technically redundant, but if we drop it then we’re
comparing pd and cd which are nonstandard and confusing
given the dual use of “d”.
> Krzysztof thinks the vertical bar and << will confuse non-programmers.

If anything “|” will confuse more programmers than users. And
“<<“ is no less intuitive for non-programmers than “+=“.
> And should that "ld" match "pdf" or vice-versa?
If we go with a more explicit choice then yes, it should become lpdf.

If we want stats paper look, e.g.

ld << cauchy(tau | 0, 2.5),

ld += normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma) -log(sigma)

ld << normal(y | mu, sigma), 1/sigma

I agree that we want the right-hand side to be any old expression.
So whatever is used for a density in place of A/B/C will just
be added to the log density.

+= is common, just not in R or BUGS or JAGS, so for
this particular audience, not so common.

I'm OK with not having a comma. You can think of it
as streaming in a vector, which is what we do now with

vector[N] x;
...
increment_log_prob(x)

which is equivalent to

for (n in 1:N)
increment_log_prob(x[n]);

So I guess another question is whether we allow vectors
on the right-hand-side of <<.

>> Krzysztof thinks the vertical bar and << will confuse non-programmers.
>

No modeling mistake, just the convention p(y | theta)
for conditional densities as opposed to p(y, theta) for
joint densities. And normal(y | mu, sigma) is the
conditional of y given mu and sigma in the sense that
for fixed sigma > 0 and any mu, it integrates to 1 over y.

- Bob

Yes, I agree with Bob that there’s a tension here. In BDA, normal(a|b,c^2) has a clearly defined meaning. In Stan, we’re changing things in two ways, and both are good: we’re moving from variance to sd parameterization (thus, normal(a|b,c)), and we’re working with log densities. In BDA notation: lp(theta|y) = const + lp(theta) + lp(y|theta). So as long as we make it clear that normal(a|b,c) is lp, we’re good. I agree with Bob that it would be good if normal(a|b,c) just represents this lp quantity. This is the cleanest way to go. And in this case I’d prefer not to have a _log suffix, as this would imply that not logging is the default. To be clean, we should never allow a density or probability function in Stan to compute a non-logged density. This just means we need to be able to handle zero density values using -Inf on the log scale. I assume we can do this?
A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] log densities
parts:
Yes, we can use -inf on the log scale, but that
causes rejection and is always due to either a misspecified
model or arithmetic issues resulting in what Michael (and now
Stan) calls "divergent" transitions.

How do we make it clear that normal(y | mu, sigma) means
what everyone else writes as "log(normal(y | mu, sigma))"?
I was originally leaning toward having normal() be
a synonym (alias) for for normal_lpdf(), but now I'm
leaning toward it being too confusing if it's not packed
right into the name. They might not know what "lpdf" means
at first glance, but at least it'll indicate that there's
something going on.

Took me a while to unpack lp as log p() and the rest as Bayes's rule:
> lp(theta|y) = const + lp(theta) + lp(y|theta)

I don't see how that's relevant.

We don't have the non-log forms of the densities because they're
so unstable arithmetically. We do have the non-log forms of the CDFs,
but I think that's a mistake in retrospect for the same reason.
The only problem is that we don't have the kind of numerical algorithm
expertise (or perhaps interest) to write stable log CDFs and log CCDFs
with derivatives.

- Bob

The way Boost is templated, we can autodiff the approximation
to function foo(x). But precision bounds on foo(x) don't tell
us anything about precision bounds on the derivative foo'(x)
resulting from autodiffing the approximation to foo().

The right thing to do is develop a new approximate algorithm for
foo'(x). But Boost hasn't done that. Ditto for inverse CDFs.

For example, differentiating beta_cdf(y, alpha, beta) w.r.t. y
is easy, but it's much trickier w.r.t. alpha and beta.

- Bob

We didn't really have a quorum for this discussion.

Andrew's opinion during the meeting was:

a) always compute normalization terms for output of log-density;
never compute normalization where not needed in the model block;
continue to include normalization in generated quantities

b) everything is on the log scale and there simply aren't
non-log-scale functions, so they don't need to be marked

Both of these are contentious points.

Daniel suggested doing (a) without too much overhead by just recomputing
the model block once per iteration using double values.

If Andrew gets his way, that'd be:

normal_pdf(y | mu, sigma) : log density

normal_cdf(y ??? mu, sigma) : log cdf

normal_ccdf(y ??? mu, sigma) : log ccdf

normal_inv_cdf(y ??? mu, sigma) : log inverse cdf

This would change the behavior of the existing functions normal_cdf()
in a non-backward-compatible way.

Then I believe Andrew wanted to allow "normal" as an abbreviation
for "normal_pdf".

- Bob
